title: U.S. House · Vermont At-Large
area: The entire state of Vermont, which has a single at-large U.S. House district.

context.text: Incumbent Becca Balint (D) advanced from the Democratic primary on August 11, 2026 with 98.3% of the vote. Gerald Malloy defeated Mark Coester in the Republican primary with 76.6% of the vote.

candidates.name: Becca Balint
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 11 Democratic primary with 98.3% of the vote

summary.text: Becca Balint is the Democratic incumbent U.S. Representative for Vermont's at-large district, seeking a third term. A former middle school teacher, she served in the Vermont Senate from 2015 to 2023, including as majority leader and president pro tempore, before winning the House seat in 2022. She serves on the House Judiciary and Budget committees.

background.text: Born May 4, 1968, at a U.S. Army hospital in Heidelberg, West Germany, and raised in Peekskill, New York; her official biography describes her as the daughter of a working-class mother and an immigrant father.

Earned a B.A. from Smith College (magna cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa), a master's degree in education from Harvard University (1995), and a master's degree in history from the University of Massachusetts Amherst (2001).
Moved to Vermont in 1994 and worked as a teacher, including fourteen years teaching middle school in Windham County, in public and private schools.
Elected to the Vermont Senate from Windham County in 2014 and served from 2015 to 2023; she was majority leader from 2017 to 2021 and president pro tempore from 2021 to 2023.
According to her official biography, as Senate majority leader she led passage of the state's first gun safety laws and of a major housing investment.
Won the 2022 election for Vermont's at-large House seat, succeeding Rep. Peter Welch, and took office in 2023; she is the first woman and first openly LGBTQ person to represent Vermont in Congress.

In the House, serves on the Judiciary Committee (including its Constitution and Limited Government and Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust subcommittees) and the Budget Committee; her official biography lists her as Vice Ranking Member of Judiciary.
Is a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus (Vice Chair for New Members), co-chair of the Congressional Equality Caucus, and vice chair of the Equal Rights Amendment Caucus.
According to her official biography, she is married to Elizabeth Wohl, an attorney and opera singer, has two children, and lives in Brattleboro, Vermont.

positions.summary: Her campaign issues page says she will fight to codify the right to abortion care in federal law.
positions.quote: Becca is a tested reproductive rights champion who will fight to codify in federal law the right to abortion care.

positions.summary: Her campaign issues page calls for expanded background checks, red flag laws and reinstating the assault weapons ban.
positions.quote: Becca believes it’s time to reinstate the assault weapons ban.

positions.summary: Her campaign issues page calls for immediate bold climate action and backs the Green New Deal to transition to a clean energy economy.
positions.quote: We need a united, 50-state solution to fighting the climate crisis – and that’s what the Green New Deal will give us.

positions.summary: Her official health care page says health care should be accessible to everyone and that she supports the Medicare for All Act.
positions.quote: Becca believes that comprehensive health care should be accessible to everyone, not a privilege for those who can afford it.

positions.summary: In a June 2026 statement on a House war powers vote, she said Congress should reassert its constitutional authority over the war with Iran, which she called unauthorized.
positions.quote: Congress cannot continue to sit on the sidelines while our country is dragged into an unauthorized war.

positions.summary: In April 2026 she chaired a Congressional Progressive Caucus task force hearing on taxing corporate greed and called for a tax code that evens the playing field.
positions.quote: we have to make sure that taxes are a way to even the playing field for Americans.

record.text: Assigned to the House Committee on the Judiciary (Subcommittee on the Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust; Subcommittee on the Constitution and Limited Government) and the House Committee on the Budget for the 119th Congress (2025-2026).

candidates.name: Gerald Malloy
candidates.ballotNote: Won the August 11 Republican primary with 76.6% of the vote

summary.text: Gerald Malloy is a retired U.S. Army officer and business executive running as the Republican nominee for Vermont's at-large House seat. A West Point graduate who served in the Army from 1980 to 2006, he later worked in government and private-sector roles, and was the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in 2022 and 2024. According to news coverage of his primary win, he is focusing on affordability and working with Gov. Phil Scott.

background.text: Born in Boston, Massachusetts; graduated from Westwood High School and lives in Perkinsville, Vermont.
Entered the U.S. Military Academy at West Point at age 18 and earned a bachelor's degree there in 1984.
Served in the U.S. Army from 1980 to 2006; in his Ballotpedia survey response he says he served 22 years on active duty and completed the Army Command and General Staff College.
Earned a graduate degree from Temple University in 1996 (described in his survey response as an MBA) and a graduate certificate from Georgetown University in 2021.

According to his survey response, after leaving the military he held government roles working with the military and then worked in the private sector, helping grow technology and service businesses; Vermont Public describes him as an Army veteran and defense contractor.
Was the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in 2022 (28.0% against Sen. Peter Welch) and 2024 (32.1% against Sen. Bernie Sanders).
Won the August 11, 2026 Republican primary for the U.S. House seat over Mark Coester, leading 77% to 22% in early returns; Vermont Public described it as his third attempt at federal office.
According to his survey response, he is married with four children; Ballotpedia lists his affiliations as including the VFW and American Legion.

priorities.text: "I will: bring high-paying jobs back to Vermont, Cut unnecessary federal regulations that hold back small businesses, Support local industries—dairy, agriculture, and manufacturing... Push for fiscal discipline in Washington to reduce inflation."

"Washington's overspending is driving inflation and making life more expensive. I will: Oppose tax increases on Vermont families, Work toward balanced budgets, Protect and strengthen Social Security and Medicare—without cutting benefits."
"I will always stand for the Constitution and the rights of every Vermonter... Uphold the 10th Amendment and states' rights... Oppose federal overreach on issues better decided locally."

positions.summary: In a 2022 Ballotpedia survey he described himself as pro-life and favored leaving the decision to the states, and in 2024 he said he would not support sweeping federal abortion legislation; his 2026 campaign Q&A says women have a right to abortion in Vermont under state law.
positions.quote: Women have a right to abortion in Vermont.

positions.summary: In a 2022 Ballotpedia survey, he said he opposes hastily implemented climate plans such as the Green New Deal and Vermont's Global Warming Solutions Act and wants to restore U.S. oil and gas independence.
positions.quote: I am passionate about establishing reasonable, realistic Energy and Environmental plans, ones that actually take into account that we do not have the infrastructure, resources, or a viable plan for every American to hastily implement plans that are full of gaps and issues, like the New Green Deal, Global Warming Solutions Act, or Climate Action Plan.

positions.summary: His 2026 campaign Q&A says he does not support the Trump administration's tariffs on Canada and wants to avoid raising costs for Vermont families and businesses.
positions.quote: No. Canada is our neighbor and an important partner for Vermont. We should stay at the negotiating table, resolve disputes, and avoid raising costs for Vermont families and businesses.

candidates.name: Phoenix Altair

summary.text: Phoenix Altair is running as an independent candidate for Vermont's at-large U.S. House seat. No biography, campaign website statements, or Candidate Connection survey responses were found on Ballotpedia.

priorities.text: Housing and healthcare as human rights.

candidates.name: Adam Ortiz

summary.text: Adam Ortiz is running as an independent candidate for Vermont's at-large U.S. House seat. He is a U.S. Army National Guard veteran (2006-2012) and was also an independent U.S. House candidate in 2022 and 2024. In his Ballotpedia 2026 Candidate Connection survey, he described environmental protection and infrastructure investment as priorities.

background.text: Born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; served in the U.S. Army National Guard from 2006 to 2012.
In a 2024 Seven Days interview quoted on Ballotpedia, he said he had deployed to Baghdad, Iraq, and then Kabul, Afghanistan.
Was an independent candidate for Vermont's at-large U.S. House seat in 2022 and 2024, losing both general elections, and is running again in 2026.

priorities.text: "All issues are environmental issues... The Vermont brand is everyone's responsibility to protect."

candidates.researchNotes: Completed Ballotpedia's 2026 survey but responses do not clearly state positions on the guide's fixed issue list.

candidates.name: Suzanne Seymour

summary.text: Suzanne Seymour is running as an independent candidate for Vermont's at-large U.S. House seat. No biography, campaign website statements, or Candidate Connection survey responses were found on Ballotpedia.

priorities.text: Oversight: eliminating fraud, waste and abuse in federal spending and maintaining Social Security.
priorities.quote: I will take a stand against fraud and abuse of federal tax dollars to minimize the federal tax burden on working Vermonters and maintain social security for retirees now and in the future.

priorities.text: Accountability: reducing the influence of large donors in elections.
priorities.quote: We need to get the Big $$ out of elections so every true candidate can be heard

priorities.text: Federal investment in jobs and infrastructure for Vermont.
priorities.quote: Vermonters need good jobs, and affordable costs.

candidates.researchNotes: Sources: her campaign site's issues page and her written answers to a Vermont Bellwether questionnaire (an independent Substack publication; the answers are printed in her own words). Her answers do not state a position on most guide issues.

statements.quote: Yes I do but I think we need to be as creative as possible about it. Instead of just building and building, Vermont could convert old barns, churches, and other existing structures into apartments instead of clearing more land for new development.
statements.context: Answering whether she supports reforming Act 250 to speed up housing development, Vermont Bellwether questionnaire (Oct. 14, 2026)

statements.quote: I believe the entire health-care system needs restructuring; it's more of a disease-care system, and we need to replace it with a preventative wellness model.
statements.context: Answering a question on the ACA marketplace, Vermont Bellwether questionnaire (Oct. 14, 2026)
